title: impermanence
hookLine: impermanence; the leaf, the mood, the year

cards: A leaf in October. Last spring it was a tight green bud. In summer it was so ordinary nobody noticed it.

Now it's red and gold and loose on the branch, and next week it'll be on the sidewalk. Set this morning's mood beside this one. Look at last year: a worry that kept someone up in March can be hard to even recall by fall.
The leaf, the mood, the year. They're all doing the same thing, at different speeds. They're passing.
The Buddha asked people to look at that, closely, until they saw it.

teach.b: Anicca. In Pali, nicca means permanent, lasting, constant. Put an a in front and you get the opposite: not lasting.
It's the first of what Buddhists call the three marks of existence, the three things true of everything that's made of parts and conditions. Anicca, impermanence. Dukkha, which you already know.
The Dhammapada puts the first one in four words: "All created things perish." Now, that sounds obvious. Everyone knows things change.
But here's the catch. It's easy to know it the way we know the sun is a star: true, and no help at all on a Tuesday. A good mood gets held as if it'll stay.
A bad week feels like forever. An ending still startles. So the Buddha didn't teach anicca as a fact to agree with.
He taught it as something to see, again and again, in small things, until it sinks in. Watch a breath: it comes, and goes. Watch a thought: it arrives, and leaves.
Watch a sound fade away. And there's another side to it. Impermanence isn't only sad news.
It's what makes change possible at all.
If things were permanent, grief would never soften.
A bad habit would never break. The seed would never grow. The same fact that takes the leaf in October brings the bud in April.

how: Buddhists reflect on anicca in meditation by watching breath, sensations and thoughts arise and pass, and in daily life by recalling that all conditioned things change; some traditions use images like falling leaves, candles and sand mandalas swept away after completion.

games.q: what's inside the word — tap the pairs.

s: it's also why grief can soften, habits can break, and seeds can grow.
anicca is the first of the three marks of existence
the Buddha taught anicca as a fact just to agree with
he taught it as something to see, again and again, in small things.

games.q: you're having the best evening in months. friends, food, a warm night. you notice it will end. what does the teaching on anicca suggest?
o: hold on tight so it lasts.
stop enjoying it. it's ending anyway.
see it clearly, passing, and be fully in it while it's here.
games.why: anicca isn't a reason to stop enjoying. seeing that the evening is passing can make you more present to it, and less crushed when it ends.

practice: The bell gives you about forty-five seconds. Watch something pass. Start with the breath: notice that each one begins, and ends, and is never quite the same as the last.
Then notice sounds around you, arriving and leaving. If a feeling comes up, watch that too. You're not trying to hold anything or push anything away.
Just watching things come and go, like leaves.

wordCard.voice: Anicca. Impermanence, the first of the three marks. Everything made of parts is passing, the hard things and the good ones. Thirteenth word.

orig.note: Pali: impermanent. a (not) + nicca (permanent). Sanskrit: anitya.

carryVoice: Your line: this passes. The leaf in October, and the bud in April. That's thirteen.
